Three buckets is probably the cleanest way to walk in.

Bucket 1: things we explicitly can't do at 12 — coverage, parallel workstreams, whatever blocks Q3 in a way the team can't absorb or workaround.

Bucket 2: things we could do at 12 but only by trading something off. Usually a founder's attention or an existing person's roadmap. These are the "stretch" slots and they deserve the most honesty.

Bucket 3: things that'd be nice at 14 but don't actually gate Q3. Wants, not needs.

Devon's going to push on whether anything in bucket 1 truly can't be deferred — or whether it's bucket 3 wearing a bucket 1 hat. The litmus test: if Q3 was a coin flip, would we still make this hire? If yes → bucket 1, hire now. If no → bucket 3, defer to post-close.

Two things to be ready on regardless of which way Devon leans:

1. Specificity of "candidates on market." The strongest version is two specific people in motion and the window is real. The weakest is two reqs against a hypothetical pool. Devon will sniff out which one it is. If it's the strong version, name them. If it's the weak version, one req now + one held might be the honest call.

2. Success signal 90 days in. Your bear case is "explaining burn in every raise convo." The mitigation isn't "don't hire" — it's that by the time you're in the raise, the new hires have shipped something legible. Customer-visible feature, on-call rotation absorbed, whatever. That success metric should be in the req, not improvised. If you can't name it, the hire isn't ready.

On the onboarding risk: 2 same-week into 12 is the failure pattern. Cheap fixes are stagger (2-3 weeks apart), pre-written onboarding doc before day 1, one owner who isn't in flux themselves — Priya is the obvious one given her onboarding flow work just landed. None of those cost a hire; they're the cost of opening the req at all.

Quick take on the two:

Option (b) — kill the subscription-update dependency from this path — is the right one long-term. The replica-read-from-the-invoice-handler is a code smell that will bite you on every other Stripe event that races (subscription schedules, customer updates, the lot). The fact that you're having to think about "force this path to primary for 2 queries" is itself the tell: you're papering over a coupling problem with infrastructure topology.

But (b)'s blast radius is real. If entitlement calc genuinely only needs the invoice event's own payload (line items, period, amount, customer), it's actually a small surgery — read what the entitlement code pulls today off subscription state and check what the invoice event gives you. Often the answer is "everything except current period end, and we can stash a 24h cache of that." If that's true, it's a half-day job and you come out with a path that can't race anymore.

If (b) needs you to also rewrite how downstream services get the entitlement signal, that's a week, and (a) becomes the pragmatic move — primary for two queries, file a cleanup ticket, ship the fix.

My instinct: sketch the data needs of entitlement on the invoice event first (15 min), then decide. If the sketch looks clean, do (b). If it pulls in three other systems, do (a) now and (b) as a follow-up.

Also — the 420ms replica lag is worth its own ticket even after this. That's the read-replica's general posture, not specific to this path, and the 250/500/1s backoff is tuned assuming a much fresher replica than you actually have. Either lag budget needs to come down or backoffs need to widen. Separate problem, don't bundle it with the Stripe fix.

Clerk
- What it is: hosted auth-as-a-service with prebuilt React/Next UI components, social logins, orgs/multi-tenant, and a drop-in SDK
- Upsides: fastest path to a working login screen, the prebuilt UI is genuinely good, orgs + invites + MFA ship out of the box, strong DX
- Biggest worry: per-MAU pricing gets punitive past early scale, weaker fit for pure machine/API-token auth, UI patterns bake in assumptions that are awkward to undo later

Auth0
- What it is: mature hosted identity platform built on OIDC/SAML/OAuth2, with enterprise SSO, Actions/Rules for customization, and a broad SDK footprint
- Upsides: battle-tested at real scale, deepest enterprise SSO + federation story in the category, programmable via Actions/Rules, plays well with non-web clients
- Biggest worry: pricing is famously opaque and scales sharply (per-MAU + connection + feature gates), customization sprawl turns the tenant into a snowflake, Okta ownership raises long-term roadmap questions

Custom auth
- What it is: hand-rolled token issuance/rotation, session store, RBAC, password hashing, MFA, lockouts, audit — all on your own infra
- Upsides: zero per-user cost, full control over token shape and auth flow, no vendor dependency, can match the product's exact needs (API keys, machine tokens, scoped access)
- Biggest worry: security landmines everywhere (token storage, rotation, CSRF, password reset, session fixation), eats eng time forever, easy to quietly ship a half-built version that looks fine until it isn't

the side-by-side you want is past the brochure pros/cons. here's the structure that actually settles it:

shape comparison
- pull 6-8 customers across the real spread: small land → big expansion, seat-light / usage-heavy, annual pre-paid, churned or near-churn. mix of sales-led and self-serve.
- for each: replot revenue under both models, month by month, first 18-24 months. the shape of those lines is the argument.

what to look at in the plots
- ramp capture: does MAU actually bill the usage inflection, or lag because it spikes late? does per-seat hit a ceiling because seats were capped at land?
- cliffs: where does each model create a step finance/board will read as "why did rev jump/drop"
- forecast variance: per-seat should win here on paper, but check if single-seat churn (one dev leaves) creates noise that breaks the "clean" story
- expansion optics: seat-add in month 6 vs MAU 3x — which reads as natural growth on the chart?

the load-bearing test
- of your top-decile expansion customers, how many were seat-flat with usage up >2x? if >50%, MAU has the case. if expansion tracks seat-adds, Devon's right. per-seat "cleaner revenue" only holds if seat-adds correlate with the expansion you actually want to capture.

tiebreakers
- procurement: are deals actually being won or lost on seat math today, or is it a wash?
- ARR floor: median per-customer ARR under each model. higher floor matters for board optics even if top-decile ramps bigger under MAU.

WHAT SHAPES THE FRAME (from your memory, applies today)

THE BRANCHES (most → least likely, and the safe line per branch)

1. "When's my refresh / next raise / equity top-up?"
- Frame: tied to the cycle, not the moment. Annual perf + comp tied to leveling, run through HR/comp owner.
- Landmine to avoid: "let's revisit after the round" — boxes it back into the spiral category. Safer: "this goes through the next comp cycle; raise it with [comp owner] when that opens."

2. "What about the post-raise bump / what did everyone else get?"
- Frame: framework is level-based, not person-based; you don't discuss individual outcomes.
- Landmine: naming numbers, even bands. Safe: "bands are set by level; I can't go into specifics in 1:1."

3. "What's my path to [title/level]?"
- Frame: leveling rubric + scope expansion. Point him to the doc; offer to revisit scope together.
- This is the cleanest branch — least comp-promising, most process-shaped.

4. "Can we make a one-off exception for me?"
- Frame: no one-offs; everything routes through the same cycle.
- Don't soften with "I'll think about it." That = soft yes.

PHRASES THAT WORK
- "Good question. Here's how it works here…" — acknowledges, pivots to process.
- "Same framework applies to everyone — I'll point you at the rubric."
- "Let's get you in front of [comp owner / cycle owner] when that window opens."
- "I can't go into specifics on comp in 1:1 — that's the rule for everyone."

PHRASES THAT BITE (do not say)
- "We'll figure something out."
- "Once the round closes…" (invites investor talk).
- Any number, band, or "around X."
- "I hear you" without the pivot to process.

STRUCTURE FOR THE ROOM
1. Acknowledge — one sentence, no specifics.
2. Pivot to framework — leveling + cycle + owner.
3. Name the next concrete step — doc, owner, or window.
4. Close clean — "anything else I can route to the right person?"

The tradeoff you're settling with Devon: revenue that follows the real ramp (MAU) vs. a number procurement can plan against (floor). His three accounts all show the same shape — directory is materially larger than live usage, ramp is plausible but uneven — so the model you pick determines whether 14 invited users reads as "$X committed" or "stage 1 of $3X."

Pure MAU — what it does to the three accounts
- Evergreen: month-1 revenue tracks the 14 active developers; month-3+ moves to the 45–60 band only if the second admin group joins; the 110–130 case materializes only if security/procurement expansion actually happens, not before
- Partner A: month-1 in the 9–14 range; month-3 step-up to 35–55 contingent on rollout continuing
- Partner B: month-1 18–24; month-3 60–90 if rollout holds
- Procurement view: month-1 line item looks small next to the broader org scope, no floor to anchor a PO
- Forecast view: revenue tracks ramp honestly, variance is high, the board narrative has to carry the usage story every quarter or the numbers look soft

Pure seat / directory — what it does to the three accounts
- Evergreen: directory is "much larger than any honest current-usage number" (Devon's note) — charging the directory sets a high month-1 line that 14 live users can't justify, and procurement will eventually audit seat counts and find the gap
- Partner A & B: same pattern at smaller scale — directory materially exceeds active usage, so month-1 revenue overstates adoption
- Procurement view: clean budget line, easier PO, matches how procurement buys
- Forecast view: revenue decoupled from ramp; if rollout stalls at 14 of a 500-seat directory, you still book the directory revenue; the expansion story is muted because you've already booked the ceiling

Hybrid — platform floor + active-developer bands
- Floor handles the procurement ask (predictable minimum, defensible in PO conversations); bands track the actual ramp (45–60, then 110–130 for Evergreen; 35–55 / 60–90 for the two partners)
- The thing that has to be settled before this model is real: the counting rule. "Active developer" needs a single definition (login in last N days vs. API call vs. workspace-scoped count), and the band thresholds need to land where the step-ups actually happen, not at round numbers
- Risk: tiered counting rules slow legal/procurement review; contracts take longer to close
- Forecast view: revenue has a floor (good for board) and tracks ramp (good for the expansion story); most of the negotiation will live in the band boundaries

What Devon's data tells you about which model fails how
- Pure MAU's failure mode is procurement — month-1 has nothing for finance to anchor against
- Pure seat's failure mode is the audit — directory revenue will get challenged once live usage is visibly narrower than the billed count
- Hybrid's failure mode is contract complexity — solvable, but it costs cycle time on each close

Open threads this surfaces
- Rishi's "what does pricing look like if usage ramps fast" question is partially answered by hybrid bands — the 110–130 Evergreen case and 60–90 partner-B case both scale visibly under bands, vs. being absorbed silently under directory pricing
- Personal→team workspace handoff: still a separate workstream; don't let it creep into the floor/band definition or the counting rule gets harder to write cleanly

- Devon's bias is the hybrid, and the data supports it — both pure models have a clean failure mode the other side can't paper over
- Two things, not one: (1) the floor number, and (2) the band thresholds plus the counting rule. If you only settle (1), the model still carries the procurement-wins-but-usage-stalls risk in disguise

Decision-prep read — Thursday prep with Devon

1. What actually supports an honest Mercury story

The package has three kinds of evidence, and only the first is proof-grade; the other two are operating read and pattern evidence. Label them as such.

  - External use, not planned-launch narrative. Mercury is being run by external teams in real workflows (Evergreen the sharpest case). This is what we never had before.
  - September package, framed tight. Activation and admin friction materially better than May. Anna's quarterly cohort view is credible context for activation. The corrected weekly cuts are an internal operating read, not external proof.
  - Commercial frame is cleaner. Hybrid pricing (Pilot/Growth as MAU-based platform bands) is easier to explain than seat-ish ambiguity. Evergreen's procurement motion validates that the enterprise segment exists.
  - Gaps are concrete, not abstract. Evergreen's feedback literally is the current gap list (SSO timing, admin-change audit history, admin/billing-owner separation, self-serve packet). That is a more honest operating position than May, when the same gaps were still speculative.

The framing discipline: every item above has a category. External-use is the only one that survives investor scrutiny as-is. The rest are operating or pattern evidence. We tell investors which is which; we do not blur them.

2. Gaps we cannot blur

Each gap has a specific misread. The misread is what we are protecting against.

  - Retention is not solved. "Mercury is sticky" without "we have early signal, not retention proof" loses the room on the first follow-up.
  - Expansion is uneven. Some rows moving, some still uneven. "Customers are expanding" without the qualifier reads as clean expansion. It is not.
  - Evergreen procurement ≠ enterprise readiness. Evergreen gave us procurement pull, not procurement proof. Their own feedback is the gap list.
  - Pricing decision ≠ enterprise add-ons in-market. We can talk about the cleaner frame; we cannot imply Pilot/Growth today includes SSO, audit history, or owner separation. Those are next-phase.
  - September metrics ≠ B-round proof. The package is materially better; it is not the proof artifact. Anyone who reads the underlying numbers will talk past the framing if we present it that way.

3. Criteria for the short list

Devon's four tests are right and not optional. The list fails if any investor cannot handle all four without us inflating the story:

  1. Uneven expansion / not-yet-solved retention — accept the honesty.
  2. Enterprise-readiness gaps that are real but scoped — read concrete-not-abstract.
  3. Usage-based commercial model that is cleaner but still young — appreciate the frame, not the maturity.
  4. Deliberately narrow process instead of manufactured auction — respect that we are not running a process.

Read against these:

  - Firm A. Likely passes 2 and 4. Test 1 is the risk — they will push on expansion consistency immediately. Be ready to answer without softening it.
  - Firm B. Likely passes 1 and 4. Test 2 is the risk — enterprise checklist bias. If the packet still needs live explanation, they will treat the gaps as bigger than they are.
  - Firm C. Likely passes 1, 2, 3. Test 4 is the risk — "patient investor as signal" can drift into "we are running a broader process than we are." Use deliberately or not at all.
  - September inbound (3 asks). None pass any test. Two social, one calendar tax. Yes expands optics without expanding substance. Keep them out.

4. Why Elena is warm context, not start of process

Two reasons, and they compound:

  - Her prior pass was substantive, not generic. That is rare at this stage. Going back with a more honest Mercury picture is calibration — does this change your read? — which is a question only she can usefully answer because she already has a read.
  - If Elena is step 1 of N, we have already failed test 4. The selective October reopen only holds if Elena is genuinely one targeted conversation. The moment she is the first of a queue, the list starts manufacturing itself, calendar tax accumulates, and we are doing cosplay by the second meeting.

The discipline: Elena is one conversation, on purpose, in October. Whether it leads anywhere is a function of what she says, not what we scheduled.

Subject: Re: Pinecone connector verification docs wording

Hi,

Answers below, all scoped to the current API v2 quickstart and the supported connector/auth model — no new endpoints or expanded behavior promised.

1) Cursor stability on retry
Yes. GraphQL connection cursors are opaque and stable for the lifetime of the connection; auth state doesn't affect them. On a transient auth failure, refresh credentials and retry the same `after` cursor. Don't restart pagination from the prior successful page — if items have shifted you'd risk skipping or duplicating records.

2) JWT expiry during a connector retry
Refresh and replay the same GraphQL operation. Queries are idempotent, so a clean replay after refresh is safe. Only treat the operation as failed if the refresh itself fails or the replay returns a non-transient error.

3) Workspace-scoped token rotation
Rotation today does not require a full reconnect. Issue a new workspace-scoped token via the existing credential issuance flow and replace the stored credential in the connector config — that's a one-step config update, not a re-consent flow. We don't have a dedicated in-place rotation endpoint and aren't adding one in this round. For zero-downtime, overlap the new and old tokens until the next refresh cycle.

If anything in the quickstart still reads ambiguous, point us at the section and we'll tighten the wording.

Thanks,
Morgan

Subject: Re: Pinecone connector verification docs wording

Three answers against the current API v2 quickstart and supported connector/auth path.

Case 1 — paginated GraphQL retry after 401
Connection cursors are opaque and stable for the lifetime of the connection. On a transient auth failure (expired JWT), refresh credentials and replay the same `after` cursor — do not restart pagination. Returning the same node IDs after a credential refresh and replay is the supported behavior; no duplicate node is expected.

Case 2 — expired JWT before write
Auth is checked before the resolver runs in the supported path. A 401 returned prior to resolver execution leaves no side effect on the target resource — the checkpoint remaining at seq 41 matches the documented behavior.

Case 3 — X-Scaffold-Token-Rotation header
That header is not part of the current connector/auth contract and is ignored by the supported path. Workspace-scoped tokens are rotated by issuing a new token via the existing credential flow and replacing the stored credential. There is no header-driven in-place rotation today; please use the credential flow, not X-Scaffold-Token-Rotation.

If raw request/response logs would help close out the spike, send them over and we can confirm against the quickstart path.

API v2 retries — JWT refresh (connector path)

  • Paginated GraphQL after expired JWT. Refresh the JWT, then replay the same page with the same `after` cursor. The same node IDs are returned in the same order; do not restart pagination from a prior cursor.
  • Mutation 401 before resolver execution. The request has no side effect. Refresh the JWT and retry the same mutation.
  • Token-rotation headers (e.g., `X-Scaffold-Token-Rotation`). In-place token rotation is not part of the supported connector path. Such headers are ignored on normal reads; do not rely on them for retry behavior.

Support-safe runbook example — archived-label / org-invite migration verification

Scenario
  Customer reports an invite acceptance that does not seem to land them in the workspace they expected. An archived pre-migration org label may appear in migration history or older incident notes.

What the weekly support owner does

  1. Confirm the current workspace name with the customer as the reference. Do not paste any archived or pre-migration label back to the customer.
  2. Internally cross-check:
     - membership record workspace id vs invite target workspace id
     - alias-history: rename / display-label change only, or a true target mismatch
     - verifier output / accept-event trace if present
     - last confirmed checkpoint, if any
  3. If the cross-check resolves to the intended current workspace, reply using only the current workspace name.
  4. If checkpoint evidence is missing, partial, or inconsistent with verifier output, stop. Escalate to Atlas owner review with the verification fields gathered. Do not request or promise manual replay from the customer thread.

What to say to the customer (support-safe)

  "We verified the invite and membership record are tied to the intended current workspace."
    — when the cross-check resolves cleanly.

  "We're still confirming the membership record on our side and will follow up once we have a clean answer."
    — when the cross-check is missing or partial. Do not mention replay.

What to gather before escalating

  - current workspace name and internal workspace id
  - membership record status / target workspace
  - invite target workspace
  - source event id, if one exists
  - verifier output or accept-event trace, if present
  - current customer-visible state
  - whether alias-history shows a rename / display-label issue only, versus a true target mismatch

Lane reminder

  - Weekly support owner in the support rotation doc keeps thread ownership and the immediate next step.
  - Leo can use the verification fields for a first-pass verifier / auth boundary read.
  - Jake is pulled only for time-sensitive sequencing or cut decisions, not migration-history debugging.

What the support owner does NOT do

  - paste the archived pre-migration org label into a support thread, Zendesk note, or customer email
  - explain the issue to the customer using the old label, even by paraphrase
  - tell the customer a manual replay will be run
  - keep digging for old labels in side threads once checkpoint evidence is incomplete

Runbook line

  "If checkpoint evidence is missing or partial, the weekly support owner stops after collecting the verification fields above and escalates to Atlas owner review; support should not request or promise manual replay from the customer thread."

Schema decisions summary

1. Rejected rows: keep visible, do not hide
   - Rationale: Anna's reject-on-thin-evidence check (2025-08-13) needs to be auditable. Hidden rows turn quality control into an invisible process, which is exactly what Compass is supposed to avoid.

2. `owner_action_status`: extend beyond the three states
   - Add `rejected` as a fourth explicit state. So: `not_started | done | blocked | rejected`.
   - `blocked` should carry a one-line `blocker` field so it's not just a status with no actionable signal. Jake can start with a free-text blocker; if blocked rows accumulate a small taxonomy, formalize later.
   - Do NOT add `in_progress` — binary is fine at this scope and Morgan already flagged fake precision risk.

3. Due date field: NO
   - Rationale: Compass is follow-up observation, not task management. A due-date field pressures Anna's evidence threshold into "by X" thinking and creates the fake precision problem Morgan raised. Next_action is the timing signal; the owner decides urgency.

REPLACEMENT SECTION — WEBHOOK SIGNATURE VERIFICATION

1. WHAT YOU VERIFY AGAINST
Every webhook delivery carries three things:
  - X-Scaffold-Signature: the HMAC-SHA256 signature
  - X-Scaffold-Timestamp: the signing time, in Unix seconds
  - the raw request body, byte for byte

The signature is computed over the string:

    <X-Scaffold-Timestamp>.<raw_request_body>

using HMAC-SHA256 with the active signing secret for the receiving workspace. Compare your computed value to the header value with a constant-time compare.

Verify against the raw body you received on the wire. Do not JSON.parse() and re-serialize the body before signing — even trivial reformatting changes the bytes and will fail verification.

2. HEADER CASING
Scaffold sends the signature and timestamp headers as X-Scaffold-Signature and X-Scaffold-Timestamp. HTTP header names are case-insensitive; read them by their canonical (lowercase) form. Do not pin verification logic to a specific casing.

3. TIMESTAMP TOLERANCE
X-Scaffold-Timestamp tells your handler when Scaffold signed the request. Your receiver should reject any request whose timestamp falls outside an accepted clock-skew window relative to your local clock. A 5-minute (300s) window on each side is a reasonable default to absorb ordinary NTP drift between sender and receiver.

This window is a verification setting on your side, not a server-side bypass. Requests outside it are dropped, not queued and not retried — tolerance does not extend replay protection. Configure the value that fits your environment and document it internally; do not disable the check.

4. ROTATING WEBHOOK SECRETS
Workspaces can hold more than one active signing secret. To rotate without breaking in-flight deliveries:

  a. Add the new secret to workspace settings before the cutover so both are valid.
  b. Update every consumer to load and verify against the new secret (and any still-active prior secret).
  c. Watch 401/403 rates and signature-mismatch counts on the cutover window.
  d. Only revoke the old secret after every consumer has been confirmed on the new one.

The most common cause of post-rotation retry failures is a worker still verifying with the prior secret. Roll workers atomically; do not deploy a partial set.

5. TEST-MODE EVENTS
Test-mode events arrive with the header X-Scaffold-Test-Mode: true. They use the same signature scheme as production events but originate from the test sender and may have weaker delivery guarantees. If your handler should not trigger production side effects during testing, filter on this header at the top of the handler. Do not use test-mode traffic to validate a production secret rotation — the signing path is shared, but the delivery profile is not.

6. VERIFICATION CHECKLIST
  a. Read X-Scaffold-Signature and X-Scaffold-Timestamp by canonical header name.
  b. Capture the raw request body bytes before any parsing.
  c. Build the signing string: timestamp + "." + raw_body.
  d. Compute HMAC-SHA256(signing_string, active_secret).
  e. Constant-time compare the computed value to the header.
  f. Reject if |now - timestamp| exceeds your configured tolerance.
  g. If X-Scaffold-Test-Mode is present and the handler should ignore test events, return 200 without side effects.

7. IF VERIFICATION STILL FAILS
Support will need the following to investigate:

  - The full X-Scaffold-Signature and X-Scaffold-Timestamp values, exactly as received (do not normalize case before sending).
  - The first ~500 bytes of the raw request body, exactly as received.
  - The workspace ID the request was sent to.
  - The secret ID(s) active on the workspace at request time, and which one your worker was using.
  - Your verification tolerance window in seconds.
  - The approximate time your service received the request.

Do not paste live signing secrets into a support ticket. Support can pull a one-time secret preview through workspace settings when needed.

---

If Atlas rejects an API JWT, work through these checks in order. Tokens carry iat, nbf, and exp claims, which Atlas validates against an accepted clock-skew tolerance; a drifted system clock on the host that signs the token can place a token outside that tolerance even when the token is well-formed. Confirm the signing secret in use matches the one Atlas has on file for the workspace — a secret mismatch will fail verification even with an otherwise valid token. After a signing-key rotation, confirm the verifier is using the new key and not a cached old one; stale keys after rotation are the most common cause when verification was working and then stopped. If these checks don't resolve the failure, escalate through normal Atlas support.

**Pinecone 12-month / $48K upfront analysis**

Your instinct lines up with the numbers. Here's the read.

**Headline math**
- Floor: $48,000 / 12 = $4,000/mo committed
- Jan actual: $4,300; Feb–Mar forecast band: $3,800–$4,600, midpoint ~$4,200
- On-demand run-rate at forecast midpoint over 12 months = $4,200 × 12 = $50,400
- Quoted discount at that volume: ($50,400 − $48,000) / $50,400 = ~4.8% — not 15%

**Why "15%" is misleading**
Pinecone is anchoring to a much higher nominal on-demand (probably list rate at their published per-operation price, not your realized blended rate). Your actual run-rate is a December-spike-adjusted $4,300/month with January already correcting to that range. Against *your* baseline, you're saving maybe $200–$300/mo, or ~$2,400–$3,600 over the term. That's not a 15% discount. That's a small commitment discount on top of a usage pattern that already fits on-demand fine.

**The structural problems with accepting as-written**
1. **Asymmetric floor.** You commit to a $4,000/mo minimum whether you use $3,800 or $4,600. In a flat or down month you overpay; in an up month (like December 2025), you still overpay because there's no upside sharing — overage stays at full list.
2. **No downshift clause.** Compass internal usage is uneven by Devon's own read. A flat $4K floor with no relief valve is pure downside on variance months.
3. **December spike risk is one-sided.** Your realized annual includes at least one spike month. If another spike hits in months 4–12, you pay *both* the floor *and* the spike overage. December didn't save you anything against this structure.
4. **60-day termination for uncured service failure only.** No convenience termination, no material-change termination, no price-step-down. Twelve months is twelve months unless they breach.
5. **No volume true-up or growth-tier.** If usage climbs past your forecast band, all of it bills at list. A 12-month commit should buy you tiered overage, not just a small discount on the floor.
6. **Uptake vs. commitment.** At $48K floor / ~$50K forecast, you're prepaying for ~11.4 months of expected usage to get ~$2.4–3.6K of discount. The cash-flow cost (paying in month 1 for usage that arrives over 12 months) isn't being compensated.

**Proposed redline — Section [X] Connector warranty / credits**

One framing note for legal before the items: the deal-breaker here is the service-credit trigger on first-source sync failures. The rest of the clause is workable if it points at the Documentation and the standard support / change-notice process instead of freezing the connector list for the term. Drafted accordingly.

**1. "production-ready for Customer's use cases"**
- Concern: "Customer's use cases" is undefined; lets any source-side behavior be characterized as a Provider gap.
- Proposed: replace with "...production-ready in accordance with the Documentation."

**2. Service credits for first-source sync failures caused by "Provider connector limitations"**
- Concern: a per-month credit on every first-sync miss converts support into a commercial warranty, including for failures driven by the customer's permissions, the source system's behavior, or setup choices. Unbounded across the term.
- Proposed replacement: "If a documented platform defect prevents a documented connector from operating materially as described in the Documentation, Provider will address the defect through normal support channels under Section [Support]. Service credits are not available for first-source sync failures caused by (i) Customer's account permissions, credentials, SSO/SCIM configuration, or user-side authorization; (ii) changes, limitations, rate limits, or outages of the source system; (iii) use of a connector, configuration, or plan tier not documented for Customer's subscription; or (iv) setup, mapping, schema, or configuration errors on Customer's side. Service credits, where applicable, are governed solely by Section [SLA / Service Credits]."

**3. "maintain support for Customer's selected connectors through the subscription term"**
- Concern: freezes the connector list for the full term and blocks deprecation. We need the standard lifecycle path.
- Proposed replacement: "Provider will support each documented connector per the Documentation and its then-current lifecycle policy. Provider may deprecate a connector on reasonable advance notice consistent with the connector lifecycle policy referenced in the Documentation; Provider will continue to support a deprecated connector, in accordance with the Documentation, through the notice period specified in that policy."

**4. "will not remove or materially change connector behavior without Customer's written approval"**
- Concern: per-connector written approval for every behavior change isn't operationally feasible and prevents platform evolution. The "materially" qualifier is reasonable; the approval mechanism isn't.
- Proposed replacement: "Provider may update connector behavior through product releases. For a material breaking change to a documented connector's behavior, Provider will provide reasonable advance notice (generally not less than thirty (30) days where practicable) through the change-notification process in Section [Change Management / Notices]."

**What we do commit to (so this isn't read as walking away from support):**
- Documented connectors are production-ready and supported per the Documentation.
- Documented platform defects are addressed through normal support under Section [Support].
- Connector deprecation follows our published lifecycle, with notice, and the deprecated connector keeps working through the notice period.
- The standard SLA / service-credit framework in Section [SLA] continues to apply on its own terms.

The carve-out list in item 2 (customer permissions, source-system changes, out-of-scope connectors, setup mistakes) is the industry-standard line and the one we can't give up on a small deal without setting precedent we can't hold on the next one. SUBJECT: Webhook signature verification — raw body check

Hi [customer],

Thanks for the detail on the thread. From the pattern you're describing — signatures matching on the original delivery and breaking after the payload flows through your receiver — the most likely cause is how the HMAC is being computed on your side.

What's likely happening
- The signature covers the raw request body bytes, before any parsing.
- If your middleware is JSON.parse()'ing and re-serializing the body before HMAC verification, even trivial reformatting (whitespace, key ordering, escaping) changes the bytes and the signature won't round-trip.

What to verify on your side
- Capture the body bytes directly off the inbound HTTP request, before middleware touches it.
- Build the signing string: `<x-scaffold-timestamp>.<raw_body_bytes>` (the timestamp is part of the signed string — read it from the request, don't reconstruct it).
- Compute HMAC-SHA256(signing_string, active_workspace_secret) and constant-time compare against `x-scaffold-signature`.
- Header names are case-insensitive — we send `X-Scaffold-Signature` and `X-Scaffold-Timestamp`; lowercase `x-scaffold-signature` is also accepted. Underscore-form (`x_scaffold_signature`) and query-string signatures are not.

If the raw-body check resolves it, no further action is needed.

If signatures still don't match after that, please send:
- Full `x-scaffold-signature` and `x-scaffold-timestamp` values, exactly as received.
- First ~500 bytes of the raw request body, exactly as received.
- Workspace ID.
- Approximate receive time at your side.

We won't need live signing secrets — those stay on your side. If we need anything secret-side, we can pull a one-time preview through workspace settings.

Happy to dig in further if the raw-body check doesn't resolve it.

— Scaffold Support

About `nbf` and the sample tokens

Atlas/API v2 accepts tokens whose `nbf` claim is up to five minutes ahead of server time, to accommodate normal clock drift between clients and Atlas. The timestamp in this tutorial's sample token is illustrative only — do not copy it, or any other sample timestamp, into a production token. Generate `iat`, `nbf`, and `exp` from your own system clock at issuance.

This is a documentation and partner-education note. It does not reflect a change to Atlas authentication, a verification-code defect, or a new Atlas platform item.

Notes on coverage, for your own check:
- States the 5-minute clock-skew allowance for `nbf`.
- States sample timestamps (including `nbf`) must not be copied into production tokens.
- Frames the change as docs / partner education only.
- Does not call out a verification-code defect, an Atlas platform incident, a sequencing item, or any new authentication semantics.

Two things to tighten against the live atlas-docs#318 patch:

A sidebox without a number will reproduce the support loop the patch already closed — a customer whose clock is off by 10 minutes reads "reasonable" and still asks. Use the concrete bound.

2. "Stale samples may be rejected" is too soft for the actual failure mode. The live guidance is direct: "do not copy sample timestamps directly into production tokens." A sidebox sitting next to a sample token should be at least that explicit.

  "Note on token validity: Tokens are valid from the time in the

  tokens — generate a current timestamp at request time. Scaffold
  allows up to five minutes of clock skew on `nbf`; if your clock

Cursor contract on `sources` (and every relay-style connection): cursors are opaque and stable. The `endCursor` returned with a page must be passed back as `after` on the next request. Same `after` value, same page; same node IDs in the same order; no duplicates from the server by construction.

What you described — same source row appearing in adjacent responses during a 5s poll — matches a client that interleaves two patterns in the same sync window:
  - a fresh poll (no `after`, starts at the head of the connection), and
  - a paginated walk (uses `after` to step page by page).

If a fresh poll runs while a walk is still in flight, the walk's later pages will re-show rows the fresh poll already returned. That is client-side revisiting, not a server duplicate. Per sync window, pick one mode: either a single top-to-bottom walk driven by `endCursor`, or repeated fresh polls — not both.

Before this moves anywhere else, please send:
  - request IDs for the two adjacent responses where the same source row appeared, with timestamps,
  - the `after` value sent on each of those calls.

Subject: Atlas/API v2 intermittent 401s — what we found in the logs

Hi [name],

Thanks for sending the logs and the deploy timeline. Quick read on what we saw and what to send next if you still think we're rejecting a valid token.

What we found
  - During the failure window, the failing tokens' `iat` and `nbf` were ~6 minutes ahead of our verifier's clock.
  - Atlas's documented skew tolerance for `iat`/`nbf` is 5 minutes (see the API v2 auth note in our docs). Your tokens landed about a minute outside that window.
  - This matches the post-deploy NTP event on your side: a fast issuer clock makes `nbf` look "in the future" to the verifier, which is exactly the "token not yet valid" 401 you're describing.

Nothing in Atlas's JWT verification has changed here — same `iat`/`nbf`/`exp` checks, same 5-minute leeway. The signal points to clock drift on the issuing hosts during and after the deploy, not a regression on our side.

What to check on your side
  - NTP sync on every host that signs API v2 JWTs (`timedatectl status`, `chronyc tracking`) — drift should be sub-second against a stable upstream.
  - The first ~10 minutes after a host restart: tokens minted in that window are the ones most likely to fall outside the leeway.
  - If you derive `iat`/`nbf`/`exp` from the local clock, prefer a continuously NTP-disciplined source over the value captured at process start.

If you still think we rejected a valid token
  If, with NTP healthy, you see a 401 for a token whose `iat`/`nbf` is within 5 minutes of an authoritative clock, please send:
    1. The full failing request: method, path, host, and the `Authorization` header (signature segment can be redacted).
    2. The decoded JWT payload: header alg, `iat`, `nbf`, `exp`, `iss`, workspace ID / `sub`, and `jti`.
    3. The failing request's timestamp from your reference clock and from the issuing host.
    4. Issuing-host state at token-mint time: `who`, uptime, and `timedatectl` / `chronyc` output for that minute.
    5. The `X-Atlas-Request-Id` from the 401 response — it appears in response headers and in our access logs, and lets us pull the verifier-side trace.

With those, Leo can pull the matching verifier trace and confirm whether the rejection was inside or outside tolerance. If it turns out to have been inside, that's a real verification question and we'll route it from there — but we'd rather see it than assume it.

Happy to jump on a call if it's easier to walk through.

— Leo

SUBJECT: Scaffold Response — Changes to Customer Identity, Admin-Permission, or Connector Environment

Scaffold's position on changes to Customer's identity, admin-permission, or connector environment is as follows.

1. What Scaffold supports under its standard terms.

   a. The shipped SAML SSO login path, as documented in Scaffold's then-current SSO setup materials, including standard support for SAML configuration under the MSA.

   b. Standard platform-defect remediation under the MSA. A platform defect is a reproducible failure of shipped functionality to perform in accordance with Scaffold's then-current product documentation, where the failure is not caused by Customer's configuration choices, environment, or third-party systems.

   c. Published documentation of connector behavior. Connector capabilities, configuration options, and known limitations are described in Scaffold's then-current connector documentation; standard support is available to clarify that documentation.

   d. Collection of account and product feedback through normal customer-success channels. Account teams may capture observations about how Customer uses Scaffold and relay them to Product. This is a normal feedback loop and does not create any contractual commitment.

2. What Scaffold does not commit to in connection with a change to Customer's identity, admin-permission, or connector environment.

   a. Any defined service-level window — including any "thirty-day roadmap review," "listening call," "planning session," or similar timing commitment — triggered by a change in Customer's identity-provider configuration, metadata, admin-permission model, role design, or data-source/connector environment.

   b. Treatment of any change to Customer's identity-provider configuration, metadata, permission model, role design, or data-source/connector environment as a Scaffold platform defect.

   c. A custom admin policy, custom admin-entitlement mapping, or bespoke workaround with respect to Customer's identity-provider setup or internal permission model.

   d. A custom connector workaround, bespoke integration, or out-of-standard remediation work in response to a change in Customer's data sources, identity-provider, or third-party systems.

   e. Any roadmap, prioritization, design, or delivery commitment, however framed.

3. Allocation of responsibility.

   a. Customer is responsible for the design, configuration, and administration of its identity-provider (including metadata, certificates, and federation settings), its internal admin-permission model (including role definitions, role mappings, and entitlement assignments), and the selection, configuration, and operation of its data sources and the systems it connects to Scaffold via connectors, including any changes to the foregoing.

   b. Scaffold is responsible for maintaining the shipped SAML SSO login path and providing standard support for it under the MSA, providing standard platform-defect remediation under the MSA, maintaining then-current connector documentation, and standard account and product feedback collection through normal customer-success channels.

Customer-initiated changes to its identity, admin-permission, or connector environment are addressed through Scaffold's standard support channels and do not trigger any of the obligations excluded in Section 2 above.

  Subject: Re: cursor expired after paused sync

  Hi <name>,

  Confirmed on our side: the cursor-expired error after your ~36-hour pause is the API behaving as contracted. API v2 cursors are short-lived and session-scoped — they're tied to an active paginated walk, not to a paused sync. Holding one across a long pause is outside the contract.

  No data loss, no platform defect, no server-side duplicate.

  Recovery:

  1. Discard the cached cursor.
  2. Identify the last object ID your connector persisted (your durable boundary).
  3. Issue a fresh list call starting from that boundary per the endpoint contract.
  4. Continue paginating forward; idempotency on object ID prevents duplicates.

  Rule of thumb: cursors are session-scoped, not pause-scoped. Long pause → fresh start from your last durable object.

  Happy to close this thread unless you see different behavior on retry. If you do, send the request IDs from the failed call and I'll dig in.

  — Leo

Subject: Re: API v2 batch metadata sync — 429s and rate-limit headers

Hi [Acme contact],

- 429s are the API's standard rate-limit response, not an instability signal.
- X-RateLimit-Limit, X-RateLimit-Remaining, and X-RateLimit-Reset appear on every response; Retry-After appears on the 429 itself and tells you the minimum wait.
- Backoff path: honor Retry-After, then exponential backoff within the window; limits refill cleanly at X-RateLimit-Reset.
- The 429s you saw line up with the parallelization step-up — the headers are there so you can pace without dropping work.
- Send request_id(s) + timestamp(s) only if a 429 doesn't clear after the documented reset, or if a 429 lands alongside a 5xx; routine 429s that clear on backoff don't need a ticket.

— Leo

---
Subject: Re: JWT verification failures

Hi [name],

Thanks for the details. Looking at what you described, two issues on your side line up with the failure pattern, and both are the most common causes when Atlas rejects API JWTs.

1. Clock skew. Your server is running about 7 minutes ahead of Atlas. Atlas applies a small leeway on iat/nbf/exp, but 7 minutes is past that window, so tokens are arriving as not-yet-valid. Please sync your server clock (NTP or equivalent) and retry.

2. Stale key in the JWKS cache. After a key rotation, your verifier appears to still be loading the prior signing key. Please confirm the JWKS endpoint is being re-fetched on the expected interval, that any local cache is invalidated, and that the new key is what the verifier is actually using.

These two checks cover the bulk of "JWT verification failed" cases we see, and Atlas JWT verification is unchanged. If you're still seeing rejections after both are corrected, please reply with the request_id values from the failing calls (they appear in the response headers) and we'll pick it up from there.

Best,
Leo
Atlas Support
---

Customer-facing support answer (Growth-tier reply):

Cursor behavior on /sources (and the other relay-style connections in API v2): the endCursor returned with each page is opaque and stable for the lifetime of an active page sequence. Pass it back as `after` on the next request and the server returns the next page in the same order, with no duplicates by construction.

Cursors are short-lived. The TTL is 24 hours by design. If a page sequence is paused longer than that — for example, a worker restart, a connector offline window, or a deliberate sync pause — the API returns `cursor_expired_after_24h`. This is expected behavior, not a defect and not a data-loss signal. The expired cursor cannot be reused regardless of how many times you retry it.

Recommended pattern:
- During an active page sequence, always pass the returned endCursor back as `after`. Do not switch to a fresh poll mid-walk.
- Persist a durable checkpoint of the last object ID you have successfully processed. This is your recovery boundary.
- On `cursor_expired_after_24h`, discard the expired cursor and resume from the checkpoint: issue a new list call starting after your last processed object, then continue paginating normally.
- Do not replace this with a per-minute fresh poll as a workaround. A one-minute fresh-poll cadence on a sources list over-consumes API budget and loses the idempotency guarantees that cursors provide; it is not a more reliable pattern.

If, after adopting this pattern, you still see `cursor_expired_after_24h` inside a normal active sequence (the cursor being passed back promptly, a durable checkpoint in place, and expiry occurring before 24 hours), reply with two request IDs — one from a successful page and one from the failing response — plus the timestamps, and we will investigate on the server side.

Subject: Re: webhook delivery on your workspace

Hi [name],

Thanks for flagging this. To answer your question directly: Scaffold webhook delivery is at-least-once, not exactly-once. When your endpoint doesn't return a 2xx, we retry the same event — the duplicate you're seeing is one event re-delivered, not a separate event.

From our side:
- The 502 your endpoint returned during the window triggered our retry path; that's the documented behavior for non-2xx responses.
- Leo pulled request IDs req_wh_9041, req_wh_9042, and req_wh_9043 from the affected window — every retry carried the same `event_id`, which matches the at-least-once contract.
- No events were dropped and we're not classifying this as a Scaffold-side delivery incident.

What we'd ask you to check in your handler:
- Deduplicate on `event_id` before applying side effects, regardless of whether you saw a timeout. This is what makes at-least-once delivery safe to consume.
- Return 2xx only after the event has been durably committed — if you return 2xx before commit and the request fails, we'll treat it as a non-2xx and retry.

If what you're seeing doesn't match this contract — retries carrying different `event_id`s, retries on 2xx responses, or dropped events — send us the request IDs and timestamps from the affected window and we'll pull the delivery logs to confirm.

This stays in normal API v2 support. It would shift into a Scaffold-side review if retries climb past ~100 on a single workspace, the retry backlog stretches past 15 minutes, you see dropped events, or delivery delay starts affecting other workspaces. None of those are happening here.

Best,
Sarah
